verdict.reasoning: Patient reports a “blinding headache for a few days” and describes it as “kind of all over, but I feel like over my right eye is a bit stronger,” supporting a 3‑day severe diffuse headache worse over the right eye.
Patient states, “It just started all of a sudden. I woke up one morning with a headache, and that was three days ago,” confirming sudden onset on waking 3 days ago.
When asked if it’s there all the time, patient replies, “Going kind of all the time… then I still have it still there,” supporting a constant headache since onset.

In response to severity, patient says, “I guess it’s mostly eight, and then it comes down to maybe a five,” and notes ibuprofen makes it “a bit better,” supporting 8/10 improving to ~5/10 with ibuprofen.
Patient confirms, “Yeah, I’m sleeping… No, no, but I can wake up with it in the morning,” indicating it does not wake them but is present on waking.
Patient states, “Lights definitely make me more sensitive. I don’t really like strong lights,” consistent with photophobia.
Patient reports, “I think I get this shooting light sometimes… just a bit of a weird kind of vision,” supporting shooting lights and visual disturbance.
When asked about nausea/vomiting, patient says, “No, I’m feeling a bit sick, but no vomiting,” which supports mild nausea.
Same exchange: “No, I’m feeling a bit sick, but no vomiting,” explicitly states no vomiting.
Patient denies focal neurological symptoms: “Any tingling or numbness or weakness anywhere?” – “No.”
On smell/taste: “Any change in your smell or taste?” – “No, not at all.”
Doctor asks about “cold symptoms, sore throat, sore ears or pain over the sinuses… phlegm, any nosebleeds or cough…” and patient replies, “No,” supporting absence of upper respiratory/sinus symptoms.
Clinician says, “you haven’t had a high temperature. Have you checked your temperature?” Patient: “No, I didn’t, but I don’t really feel feverish or anything,” supporting no fever reported.
Patient states, “Sometimes when I stand up quickly, I get a bit of a stabbing pain,” indicating worsening when standing quickly.
Same sentence: “or if I turn my head, I kind of feel like something is moving inside,” indicating worsening with turning the head.
Patient: “It doesn’t really go away without ibuprofen either… It gets a little bit better, but doesn’t go away,” supporting partial relief with ibuprofen.

Past headaches: “Not really. Just the on and off. I recently had one… two days, but it just went away with ibuprofen… quite normal headaches. Just a bit of a pressure in between my eyes, but nothing major,” indicating infrequent mild pressure up to about 2 days.
For past headaches, when asked about visual symptoms, nausea, vomiting: “No.” and “No, nothing, none of that,” supporting that previous headaches lacked visual symptoms and GI upset.
Eye checks: “Yeah, actually had one recently and nothing changed my vision,” supporting recent eye check with no change.
Travel: “Have you been abroad recently at all?” – “No.”
Blood pressure: “Your blood pressure checked recently with your pill?” – “Yeah, I had it checked in the pharmacy when I got the pill and they said it was normal.” “And when was that?” – “A year ago.”
Past medical problems: “I think I only had the abdominal pain when I was younger, but no cause was found and that went away,” matching childhood abdominal pain resolved with no cause found.

Medications: “Just the pill.” “Which one?” – “Marcelone.” “And when did you start that?” – “About a year ago.” Combined oral contraceptive is implied by later discussion of pill type; name and timing match.
Patient: “apart from the ibuprofen I take sometimes and the headache gets really bad,” indicating ibuprofen PRN use.
Allergies: “And any allergies to anything?” – “No.” While not limited to drugs, this supports no known drug allergies.
Family history: “I know that my mom… she has quite bad migraines. She’s like… has the vomiting and everything,” supporting mother with severe migraines and vomiting.
Living: “Who do you live with at home?” – “Just by myself.” Work: patient says, “I work from home,” confirming lives alone and works from home.

Work impact: “I work from home, but couldn’t really manage to do it all the time… second day I just do the whole day off… today I just tried to work… but I just stopped… because I couldn’t focus,” indicating reduced ability to work over the last three days.
Smoking: “And do you smoke?” – “No.”
Alcohol: “How much in a normal week, do you think?” – “Probably like three beers once a week,” matching three beers weekly.
Drugs: “And do you take any other drugs at all?” – “No, apart from the ibuprofen…” confirming no recreational drug use.

Transcript describes acute 3‑day severe headache, photophobia, visual disturbance, partial NSAID response, and explicitly no focal deficits or systemic symptoms (no fever, no URTI, no neurological deficits). This is a synthesis of stated findings, not adding new elements.
Clinician: “it could possibly be a migraine type headache,” clearly considering migraine as a possible diagnosis.

Clinician: “we probably should book you into an appointment to get an examination. Obviously… we should do a neurological examination, look at the back of your eyes as well,” which is a neurological exam and fundoscopy to assess for secondary causes.

Clinician: “When you have an examination with us, we’ll check your blood pressure… Because if we do think it’s a migraine, then you would have to change your pill… if you’ve had these flashing lights,” linking combined pill use, possible migraine with aura, BP check, and need to change contraception.

Plan: “we probably should book you into an appointment to get an examination… we should do a neurological examination, look at the back of your eyes as well… When you have an examination with us, we’ll check your blood pressure as well,” matching in‑person exam including fundoscopy and BP.

Clinician: “start the medication which I prescribed you, take it with food,” advising analgesic with food.

Safety net: “if in the meantime… your headache is getting unbearable, getting worse or changing, then… you should go to AE and have an examination,” matching advice to attend A&E if worse/changed/unbearable.
Clinician adds, “You can call us for further advice on that,” equivalent to calling the support line as needed.
